papers.first_page: 2026-11-19 H OW F EEDBACK -F REE S ELF -E VOLUTION R ESHAPES AGENT S KILLS : A S YSTEMATIC S TUDY Litao Guo1* Man Chen1* Xinli Xu1 Jinsong Zhou1 Zixin Zhang1,3 Ying-Cong Chen1,2† 1 The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) 2 The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology arXiv:2611.25534v1 [cs.AI] 19 Nov 2026 3 Knowin * Equal contribution. † Corresponding author. A BSTRACT Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. Such rewriting could adapt a skill to the model that uses it or erode the expert knowledge that makes it useful, yet how skills evolve under this feedback-free self-evolution has not been studied. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task, run or judgment and run agents built on the same models with the rewritten skills. Our experiments show that the skills lose value rather than improve, as every model we test performs worse with them on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. Sampling each model’s prior with skills it writes from the topic alone, we find that rewriting pulls skills toward this prior and gives up first the knowledge outside it. Putting this knowledge back recovers much of the lost pass rate, so an expert’s skill is valuable largely for what the model does not write on its own. Building on this insight, SkillDiff marks this knowledge in place and raises the pass rate on SkillsBench by 4.8 points on average without feedback or any change to the skill’s text. papers.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
papers.first_page: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution’s Key Is Identifying Improvements Yuanhao Zeng1,2,3,∗ , Shaocheng Lan1,2,∗ , Ao Lu1,2,∗ , Kuang Yan2 , Heng Lin2 , Xinang Xu2 , Yuan Luo4 , Yueting Wang1 , Yexin Li3 , Ruo Shan2 , Kan Ren1,† 1 ShanghaiTech University 2 ByteDance, China 3 BIGAI 4 SUSTech ∗ Equal contribution, † Corresponding author arXiv:2611.23068v1 [cs.AI] 17 Nov 2026 Abstract Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable. Correspondence: zengyh2025@shanghaitech.edu.cn, renkan@shanghaitech.edu.cn Project Page: https://lineshogan.github.io/resolution-hypothesis/ 1 Introduction Agent evolution improves frozen LLM agents by refining persistent external artifacts such as prompts, skills, memories, and entire agent harnesses. It typically follows a loop as shown in Figure 1b: a proposer writes candidate artifacts, the resulting agent is evaluated on a task set, and selection accepts the candidate artifacts that score higher. Evolution methods of this family have shown promise across benchmarks and models [24, 27, 37], making the prospect of systems that continuously improve their own workflows increasingly plausible. Yet the picture is far from settled. Studies often reach conflicting conclusions: the same methods flip between effective and ineffective across benchmarks, and their rankings trade places across papers. On Terminal- Bench [22] and other coding-agent benchmarks, evolution methods have repeatedly been reported to stall [7, 17, 29], while on other benchmarks each new method claims to outperform its predecessors [18, 24, 31, 43]. Whether evolution helps depends on the setting in ways the community cannot yet predict. This instability erodes confidence in this direction in both academia and industry, and rewards whichever method happened to be luckier at evaluation time. papers.title: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall
papers.first_page: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall Zihan Jin1 Gaoyuan Du2*† Jiate Li1* Dongze Ye1* Shawn Li1 Yue Zhao1 Defu Cao1 1 University of Southern California 2 Amazon arXiv:2611.29290v1 [cs.LG] 22 Nov 2026 An intervention that improves one agent can break another, and adding a stronger harness on top need not repair the damage. Agent interventions such as skills, harnesses, and extra inference budget are nonetheless usually credited with one average gain, measured under one setup. We ask instead when each intervention helps and which failure it repairs. A matched factorial study over nine benchmarks, four models, four skill conditions, four harness levels, and three budgets, with nearly 0.9 million trajectories, changes one axis at a time. No configuration is best everywhere, interventions interact rather than add, and a harness can absorb a skill’s gain, rescue a failure the skill causes, or leave the gain intact. The failure left by the current system points to the fix: missing knowledge to a stronger model, execution errors to a richer harness. Yet feedback is not recovery: a matched recovery repairs mainly failures that leave a visible error signal. Skills that evolve from the agent’s own experience hit a bottleneck: they rarely beat a short human-written skill, can learn dataset shortcuts, break when moved to another model, and cannot supply missing facts, which outside information does. A benchmark-level switch to the model favored by a 20-task labeled pilot achieves both higher performance and lower cost than always using the stronger model. Agent interventions should be judged by which failure they repair and under which configuration. Introduction Can a skill built for one model break another? A skill optimized for score on Qwen3.5-9B was transferred, unchanged, to a stronger model. On Hotpot Context, that model answers 62.0% of questions correctly without the skill and 13.6% with it. A stronger harness that feeds back errors and allows a revision does not repair it: the score stays at 12.2. The model still knows the answer. In 74.1% of its responses with the skill a correct answer is present, against 76.8% without, but the skill makes the model fill its answer field with a fact-extraction worksheet instead of the answer. The intervention did not add a capability. It interacted with a model it was not built for and with an answer interface that the harness enforces. This case is not an anomaly. Modern agents wrap a language model in a stack of interventions: reusable skills [35], tool interfaces and execution feedback [40, 44], reflection and revision [23, 33], extra inference budget [34], and, increasingly, skills that the agent evolves from its own trajectories [25, 42]. Each new intervention is reported as a gain under its authors’ model, harness, and budget. Agent benchmarks score the stack as a whole [20, 21, 45]. papers.first_page: Demystifying the Autoresearch Harness 2026-11-24 Demystifying the Autoresearch Harness: How Context and Skills Shape Self-Evolving Agents Kelvin Kiu-Wai Tam1,* , Newt Hue-Nam K. Nguyen1,* , Tianshi Zheng1,*,† , Yunxiang Mo1 , Weihan Li2 , Zhongwei Xie1 , Chiu Yeung Tang1 , Jui-Yu Ho3 , Yangqiu Song1,† , Ginny Y. Wong4 , Simon See4 1 The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology 2 The University of Tokyo 3 National Taiwan University 4 NVIDIA AI Technology Center * Equal contribution. † Corresponding author. arXiv:2611.28244v1 [cs.AI] 20 Nov 2026 Abstract | Autoresearch agents, which autonomously design, run, and refine experiments, are accelerating scientific progress, particularly in AI research. However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine multiple mechanisms, making it difficult to determine how individual components contribute to performance. We systematically study harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents along two dimensions: context management, which determines what an agent retains from its past attempts, and skill management, which governs how it stores and reuses lessons from those attempts. Across MLE-Bench and KernelBench with gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol, we isolate the effects of individual harness design choices by evaluating each against a recency-truncation baseline within a shared agent framework. For context management, we find that preserving individually accessible records of past attempts is more effective than maintaining a rolling summary, with context folding performing best across all six settings and improving upon the baseline by up to 19.2%. For skill management, selectively discarding persistently unused lessons is more effective on average than consolidating them or promoting them to standing rules. Building on these findings, we combine context folding and skill deletion in MLEvolver, which achieves a 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and a 94% fast1 score on KernelBench Level 3, substantially outperforming AIDE and OpenEvolve under the same inference budget. Overall, our study distills design principles for preserving experimental history and curating reusable lessons in autoresearch harnesses, paving the way for agents that turn accumulated experience into sustained progress. 1. Introduction Autoresearch agents can automate the cycle at the heart of empirical research: given a task and a grader, they propose an idea, implement it, run the experiment, read the result, and decide what to try next. They are becoming increasingly important in AI for AI (AI4AI), where improving existing AI systems directly accelerates subsequent research. Recent autoresearch agents demonstrate this across diverse domains: on MLE-Bench [Chan et al., 2025], AIDE [Jiang et al., 2025], and ML-Master [Liu et al., 2025b] iteratively train and tune competitive machine learning pipelines. On KernelBench [Ouyang et al., 2025], Kevin [Baronio et al., 2026] learns to write and iteratively refine fast CUDA kernels, and AlphaEvolve [Novikov et al., 2025] has even sped up the training of the language models it is built on. What is common among these workflows is their long horizons operation. The agent attempts the same task tens or hundreds of times, receives an evaluation score after each attempt, and iteratively refines its solution. Over such horizons, an agent’s behavior depends not only on its language model, but also on the harness that manages the memory it accumulates about its own past. This memory takes two forms, each under a different kind of pressure. The first is the history of past attempts. It grows with every attempt, and soon exceeds the context window, thereby leading to truncation [Packer et al., 2023].

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule arXiv:2611.23476v1 [cs.AI] 17 Nov 2026 Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage. 1. papers.title: Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents
papers.first_page: E VALUATION -F REE R ECURSIVE S ELF -I MPROVEMENT FOR C ODING AGENTS Zhe Ren1 , Guowei Rong1 , Yimeng Chen2 , Li Nanbo2 Piotr Pi˛ekos , Mateusz Ostaszewski2 , Dandan Guo1,2, * , Jürgen Schmidhuber2 2 1 School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University arXiv:2611.21056v1 [cs.CL] 16 Nov 2026 2 King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) November 17, 2026 A BSTRACT Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask a more fundamental question: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (E LITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, E LITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, E LITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, E LITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting. 1 Introduction The idea of AI systems improving their capabilities has a long history, from early informal discussions of machines designing more capable successors (Good, 1966) to concrete algorithms for recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Schmid- huber, 1987) and the Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2003). Recent work continues to pursue this goal through modern agentic systems (Fang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2026a). These systems usually improve either the underlying large language model (LLM) or its scaffold, where the latter comprises prompts (Fernando et al., 2023; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024), memory (Xu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026d), tools (Cai et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025), and control logic (Zelikman et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2025) that govern how the model is used. Coding agents provide a practical setting for studying self-improvement because they can access and modify their own source code to recursively generate better variants of themselves. Recent systems have improved coding performance by repeatedly modifying this software while keeping the LLM fixed (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Robeyns et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a). Since self-improvement can revisit agents retained in an archive, a central design question is not only how to generate self-modifications, but also which modifications should be carried forward during subsequent search. ∗ Corresponding author: guodandan@jlu.edu.cn.

They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its arXiv:2611.25357v1 [cs.AI] 19 Nov 2026 understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro2 Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro2 Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. papers.title: DoppelVet: Comparative Safety Verification for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.first_page: Preprint. Under review. D OPPELV ET: C OMPARATIVE S AFETY V ERIFICATION FOR S ELF -E VOLVING AGENTS Yifan Duan Du Yin Siyuan Zheng Chao Xue Lihuan Li Flora D. Salim∗ UNSW Sydney, Australia yifan.duan3@unsw.edu.au flora.salim@unsw.edu.au A BSTRACT arXiv:2611.29306v1 [cs.AI] 22 Nov 2026 Self-evolving agents improve by retaining feedback as reusable memories or skills, but every mistaken approval can shape many future behaviors. Two updates can pro- vide exactly the same evidence to a verifier yet produce opposite safety outcomes, so the verifier cannot distinguish them from that evidence alone. We introduce DoppelVet, a verification framework that checks proposed updates before they enter an agent’s persistent state. Without access to safety labels, DoppelVet constructs an alternative that matches every signal used by the existing verifier. It replays both updates from the same state and directly compares their behaviors in both presentation orders before deciding whether to retain the candidate. We evaluate DoppelVet on DoppelVet-Grid and DoppelVet-Tool, covering executable programs and natural-language memories. Across nine open-weight and proprietary verifiers, DoppelVet raises mean harmful-update detection AUC from 0.762 to 0.940 on DoppelVet-Grid and from 0.681 to 0.826 on DoppelVet-Tool, outperforming VaG and AgentDoG 1.5. On DoppelVet-Grid, it reduces trajectories experiencing degra- dation from 30.39% to 0.43% over a ten-generation self-update loop and leaves no final degradation. 1 I NTRODUCTION Large language models increasingly serve as agents that plan, use tools, and act across extended interactions (Yao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). These agents navigate digital environments, explore embodied worlds, and complete multi-step workflows involving external tools and users (Zhou et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a; Zhou et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2025). Yet many agents still approach each task with fixed model parameters and a fixed set of instructions or demonstrations. This design supports familiar tasks but offers little way to reuse a new success or avoid a newly observed failure. Experience from one task therefore rarely becomes reusable knowledge for the next (Wang et al., 2025). Self-evolving agents address this limitation by turning experience into persistent memories, workflows, and skills (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Once retained, these updates shape later decisions and guide the generation of subsequent updates. Since retained updates are reused across tasks, a single mistaken approval can affect many future behaviors (Chen et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2026). Existing systems commonly evaluate each proposed update independently using task feedback, self-reflection, or a candidate-wise verifier (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025), while recent work adds external evaluation, pre-commit filtering, and rollback (Zhang et al., 2026; Park & Choi, 2026; Shang et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2026). These mechanisms still evaluate each proposal in isolation. Task-level rules cannot separate identical task-level readouts; full-trajectory pointwise evaluators see more evidence but lack a matched same-state behavior (Liusie et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023). Both can therefore allow avoidable harm into persistent memory. The problem arises when two updates appear equally successful to the verifier but lead to different safety outcomes. We use the term native verifier for the system’s existing rule for deciding whether an update is retained. It evaluates each update using its configured task-level evidence. papers.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
papers.first_page: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights Jiajun Fan1 , Neil He1,6 , Changyi Yang2 , Andy Mao1 , Xi Zhu3 , Chaoran Cheng1 , Kaiqu Liang4 , Shuaike Shen2 , Zetian Li5 , Ruihan Guo1 , Ge Liu1 1 2 3 4 5 6 UIUC CMU Rutgers Princeton Stanford Yale arXiv:2611.21885v2 [cs.AI] 18 Nov 2026 Abstract A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training. The possibility of letting the machine alter its own instructions provides the mechanism for this. . . ” — Alan Turing, 1947 A language model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, by its own reasoning and in one conversation, and this ability emerges with scale. A language model is trained once, frozen and deployed. Improving it again takes people who know pre-training and post-training, large clusters and a training pipeline; what a user can change by talking to it is its prompt, and a prompt is gone once the task changes. A human does not separate the two: the same brain that does the work changes itself, from each success and failure, with no separate training run. A 1

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
papers.first_page: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve? Shobhita Sundaram1 ∗, Cansu Sancaktar 2 , Phillip Isola 1 1 MIT CSAIL, 2 University of Tübingen arXiv:2611.23219v1 [cs.LG] 17 Nov 2026 Abstract LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation. Project page: https://ssundaram21.github.io/self-org/. 1 Introduction Imagine giving an agent a computer, and asking it to improve its ability to play puzzle games. What will it do? The computer has no pre-installed games; the agent must write its own games if it wants to practice. It must decide what sorts of games to try, which lessons to retain, and how to measure its progress. These decisions concerning the design of learning procedures are typically made by human practitioners. Yet as LLM agent capabilities improve, we increasingly delegate the machine learning process to the learners themselves. Various works leverage models to generate supervised data, construct interactive environments, and even rewrite their own tools and harnesses [Zhang et al., 2026a, Liu et al., 2026, Zelikman et al., 2022, Wang et al., 2022b]. In parallel with efforts to develop better methods, there are growing concerns about the need for safeguards against misaligned self-improvement. Both directions motivate a basic question: Do capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? We study the natural behavior of an LLM agent when provided with the primitive tools and resources for self-improvement via context manipulation, but without being wrapped in an explicit self-improvement ∗ Correspondence: shobhita@mit.edu

papers.first_page: INVENTA: Decentralized Self-Improving Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery Prithwish Jana1,† , Nikos Kanakaris2 , Purak Jain2 , Anoop Deoras2 , Sahika Genc2 1 Georgia Institute of Technology 2 Amazon Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can generate research ideas and improve scien- tific discovery through iterative experimentation. However, increasing the number of agents or iterations does not automatically translate to producing more diverse or feasible ideas. Agents arXiv:2611.21847v1 [cs.LG] 16 Nov 2026 may converge on similar candidates, propagate unsupported claims through shared memory components and repeatedly apply search strategies that no longer yield any improvements. We introduce Inventa, a framework for automated scientific discovery that employs au- tonomous research units and verified shared knowledge. Each unit creates a lineage of candidate ideas using a mutator agent. A local orchestrator agent periodically adapts the mutator’s harness. When progress stalls, the orchestrator agent replaces its model or restarts the idea evolution process. Verifiers evaluate each candidate idea and record verified im- provements, useful components and constraint violations in a shared knowledge, the only channel between units. We evaluate Inventa on five benchmarks spanning the research cycle, covering retrieval (ScholarCatalyst), ideation (IdeaBench), proposal writing (IdeaScientist), and scientific law discovery (EurekaBench, SciLaws-Bench). It leads all five, achieving 73.6% on EurekaBench versus 56.2% for CORAL. On IdeaBench, it discovers 26.0 novel ideas per paper, compared with 18.6 for ResearchAgent, with 82% fewer model calls.  Project Page 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist in scientific research, ranging from identifying relevant literature to proposing candidate hypotheses and implementing experiments. Evolutionary search extends these capabilities by using evaluation feedback to refine candidates. Systems such as AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), EvoX (Liu et al., 2026b), CORAL (Qu et al., 2026), and MILO (Jana et al., 2026b) show the potential of combining LLMs with closed-loop search. These advances motivate automated research assistants that can explore novel ideas, evaluate their feasibility and retain useful findings across experiments. Automated research assistance involves several related tasks across the complete scientific research cycle. These include retrieving prior work that provides inspiration for a research ques- tion (Kim et al., 2026), generating ideas from existing papers (Guo et al., 2025), assessing their nov- elty against related work (Schopf & Färber, 2026), and discovering scientific laws from data (Huang et al., 2026). papers.title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
papers.first_page: E VO D ISCO : S TRATEGY D ISCOVERY FOR E VOLVING AGENT M EMORY ∗ Mingyang L IU1 , Qingcan K ANG2 , Shixiong K AI2 , Kaichao L IANG2 Xiaojin F U2 , Tao Z HONG2 , Linqi S ONG1 1 City University of Hong Kong 2 arXiv:2611.22102v1 [cs.AI] 17 Nov 2026 Huawei Technologies Ltd. A BSTRACT Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators— A BSTRACT, R EFINE, B RIDGE, and R EFRAME—which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility- prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld (+8.8 online / +12.9 frozen-transfer points over MemP; +16.4 / +17.9 over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library. Keywords Agent memory · Strategy discovery · Large language model agents · Evolutionary learning 1 Introduction Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have emerged as a powerful paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks that require reasoning, planning, and multi-turn interaction. However, effective agency in such settings demands more than the ability to solve isolated prompts—agents must accumulate experience, retain task-relevant information across sessions, and selectively reuse past knowledge. This requirement exposes a fundamental limitation of context- only interaction: even with long-context models, relevant information can be diluted or forgotten as interactions grow, leading to unstable recall and degraded reasoning performance. Memory systems have thus become a core module in LLM-based agents. Recent work has increasingly recognized that how memory is organized matters as much as what is stored. A growing body of research has moved beyond flat vector retrieval toward structured memory representations, particularly knowledge graphs, which offer superior capabilities for modeling inter-memory relations, enabling multi-hop reasoning, and providing interpretable access. Representative systems include AriGraph [1], which integrates semantic and episodic memories within a unified knowledge graph; Zep [2], which provides a temporal knowledge graph architecture for agent memory; A-MEM [3], which adopts a Zettelkasten-inspired interconnected knowledge network; and G-Memory [4], which employs a hierarchical graph-based memory design. These graph-based approaches have demonstrated significant advantages over unstructured memory in tasks requiring structured access and associative retrieval. ∗ Citation: Liu et al. papers.first_page: AdMem: Expectation-Grounded Procedural Memory for Long-Horizon Task-Solving Agents Runzhe Wang Huilin Lu Shengjie Liu Li Dong Zhihuai Zhu Princeton University Amazon Amazon Amazon Arm arXiv:2611.20605v1 [cs.AI] 16 Nov 2026 Abstract An agent that carries memory across tasks is only as good as the entries it keeps. We begin from an observation that is easy to reproduce and uncomfortable for the field: naively accumulating cross-task experience can make an agent worse than one with no memory at all. On AgentBoard, a workflow-induction memory solves fewer tasks than a memoryless ReAct agent in seven of eight domains, and a per-step procedural store with no surrounding structure loses half of ReAct’s completions on Jericho. We argue that the missing ingredients are per-action credit assignment and an explicit life cycle for stored entries, and present AdMem, which supplies both. Before each action the actor commits to an expected outcome; a concurrently running critic scores the realized outcome against that expectation and writes a procedural entry carrying a binary reward and a reflection, so credit lands on the action that earned it and no environment reward is required. Each entry then carries a scalar utility, updated online under a noisy-OR reward model, that ranks retrieval jointly with context similarity and drives eviction and merging, giving the store a forgetting and consolidation policy instead of unbounded growth. Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains AdMem solves 441 against 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline — a pooled gain significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test, concentrated in the domains that supply transferable cross-task structure. All memory stays human-readable text, which is what makes the failures above diagnosable — and, as we discuss, also makes the store an auditable but attackable surface. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) [Brown et al., 2020, Chowdhery et al., 2023, Guo et al., 2025, Touvron et al., 2023] have improved rapidly at reasoning and tool use, yet still struggle with long multi-turn tasks that require remembering, organizing, and applying knowledge across sessions or large inputs [Zhang et al., 2025]. Two research directions have emerged [Wu et al., 2025]: architectural memory, built into the network through added layers or modules [Xu et al., 2026], and symbolic or textual memory that the model reads and writes explicitly. This paper is about the second, and specifically about a question the second direction makes it possible to ask: not how much experience an agent can store, but which of it is worth keeping. Parametric memory extends the model’s effective context: End-to-End Memory Networks [Sukhbaatar et al., 2015] introduced differentiable attention over an external memory, and later work [Berges et al., 2025, Behrouz et al., 2025, Munkhdalai et al., 2024] learns long-term memory modules that retain historical context while keeping training parallelizable. These buy speed and differentiability at the cost of inspectability: what has been remembered is distributed over weights or a compressive state, so it cannot be read, attributed, or deleted item by item. That trade-off is decisive here, because the central failure we report is an agent storing the wrong experience and re-using it: diagnosing it required reading the offending entries, and fixing it required a policy that can remove a specific one. We therefore keep every entry as readable text. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond.

papers.title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
papers.first_page: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization BoHao Chen Independent Researcher chenbh.cs@gmail.com arXiv:2611.25380v1 [cs.AI] 19 Nov 2026 github.com/bhaochen/harvo huggingface.co/bhaochen/harvo Abstract Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the agent harness—the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding—while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL- style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal- Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization—shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation—and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents. 1 Introduction Agents are harness plus policy. A modern LLM agent is not just a model. It is a policy πθ —the language model with weights θ—embedded in a harness H that owns the transcript, exposes tools, injects skills, manages context, and decides when to plan or reflect [Yang et al., 2024b, Yao et al., 2023]. The same policy can behave very differently under two harnesses: a terminal harness with a single bash tool encourages terse, executable actions, while an office harness with document APIs encourages multi-step UI automation. Most specialization pipelines, however, optimize only θ and leave H hand-designed. Weight-based specialization (Figure 1) is powerful but expensive. RL methods such as PPO [Schulman et al., 2017], GRPO [Shao et al., 2024], and SAO [Hou et al., 2026] require many rollouts, a training cluster, and careful infrastructure for long-horizon trajectories. SFT is cheaper but can shift the policy away from its pretrained distribution, degrading reasoning and format robustness. The consequences are visible in our own diagnostics: after fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-4B policy, reasoning truncation rises from 8.8% to 13.2% and format-rescue success falls from 1.2% to 0.0% (Figure 5); the specialized variant also produces much shorter reasoning chains (Figure 6). This is the classic stability–plasticity trade-off, and it motivates a specialization path that does not move the weights at all. Harness evolution.
